title: Anthropic Hands Over 5% of Its Equity as the AI Sell-Off Hits Asia's Memory Makers
subhead: Anthropic creates a public benefit fund holding 5% of its shares, scaling with its valuation, while CXMT falls 6-8% despite strong earnings and Kioxia faces margin-call pressure. The AI trade is being repriced by its financing, not by demand.

sections.heading: Anthropic Turns Equity Into a Public Benefit Fund
sections.body:
Anthropic said on Sunday it will commit 5% of its shares to a new 'public benefit fund', structured as a wholly-owned entity inside the company, with the option to add another 2% for every 50% increase in Anthropic's value, according to TechCrunch and BBC. The company floated uses including 'large donations to traditional nonprofits or direct distributions to specific populations', on top of the $200 million it has already committed to studying AI's effect on jobs. Governance and structure details are promised in the coming months.

The timing matters. The announcement lands as Anthropic courts investors ahead of a stock market debut (BBC reported on those talks last week) and as CEO Dario Amodei describes public sentiment toward AI as 'fundamentally a crisis of trust', per TechCrunch. Putting equity rather than cash into the fund means the payout grows with the company, but it also gives Anthropic a visible answer to the question regulators and the public are asking: who benefits when these companies get very large.
sections.whyItMatters: A 5% perpetual claim on the most valuable private AI labs is a new instrument in AI governance, created by the labs themselves rather than by legislation. It sets a benchmark competitors will be asked to match.

sections.heading: China's Memory Champion Posts Big Numbers and Falls 8%
sections.body:
CXMT, China's leading DRAM maker, reported a strong earnings turnaround but its shares dropped more than 6% in Shanghai trading on Monday (CNBC), following an 8% fall on Sunday/HK time according to SCMP. Investors are looking past the profit number. SCMP reported last week that China's self-sufficiency push and the domestic AI boom had fuelled an earnings surge across local chip firms; the sell-off suggests that surge is already priced in.

In Japan, Kioxia shares are under pressure from margin buying that went wrong, the Japan Times reported on Monday, a mechanical unwind rather than a verdict on the NAND market. Both moves are part of the same pattern: the AI hardware trade is now being driven by positioning and financing costs rather than by order books.
sections.whyItMatters: China's memory industry is genuinely earning money now, but its stocks are trading like momentum assets. The gap between industrial progress and market pricing is the story in Asia this week.

sections.heading: The AI Buildout's Problem Is Debt, Not Demand
sections.body:
The Financial Times ran two pieces over the weekend on the same theme: America's $10 trillion AI infrastructure boom is starting to fray, and Microsoft has pulled out of a data centre deal with Nscale (FT). CNBC reported that tech stocks plunged and inflation heated up. The Guardian reported the sell-off deepened amid fears over US inflation and AI debt.

On the physical side, the buildout is not slowing. SemiAnalysis analysis cited by Tom's Hardware found that of more than 400 local moratoriums across 17 states, only about 2.3 GW of roughly 21 GW in affected areas is likely to be delayed, against 38 GW of US data centre IT capacity projected for 2027 - more than double 2026. Their conclusion: 'Moratoriums are much more bark than bite.'
sections.whyItMatters: The constraint on AI capacity this quarter is the cost of capital and local politics, not chips and not concrete. A single cancelled hyperscaler deal says more about 2027 supply than any number of county bans.

sections.heading: Ukraine Knocks Out Russian Digital Services by Hitting Data Centres
sections.body:
Over the past week Ukrainian drones struck some of Yandex's largest data centres, disrupting shopping, taxi and other metro digital services across major Russian cities, Tom's Hardware reported. Yandex facilities house two of the country's top supercomputers. Cloudflare analysis found Russian bot and disinformation traffic did not collapse; it 'auto-migrated' to other hosts, so the operational effect on information operations was smaller than initial reports suggested.

The numbers are the point: a handful of Yandex data centres support a very large share of Russia's consumer internet. Russia has also struck Ukrainian data centres in recent weeks, but Ukraine's reliance on distributed Western cloud services has proved harder to knock out than Russia's concentrated domestic platforms.
sections.whyItMatters: Data centres are now a military target set, and concentration is a vulnerability. Countries that run their consumer internet through two or three domestic providers are exposing a single point of failure to drone strikes.

sections.heading: Europe Learns the Same Lesson From Its Fridges
sections.body:
POLITICO reported on the cyberattack that remotely raised temperatures on refrigerators in hundreds of French supermarkets, forcing Intermarché and Carrefour stores to throw away defrosted food and spoiled milk. It is arguably the most consequential hack in the EU this year. French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu personally managed the fallout. Experts quoted by POLITICO say the hackers most likely used ordinary methods - internet-exposed controllers - rather than AI; Claroty had identified a flaw in a Danfoss refrigeration controller, which Danfoss fixed in 2025.

Dutch food security minister Silvio Erkens noted unrelated incidents at Dutch and Belgian supermarkets the same week, and pointed to how heavily the food chain depends on IT. A French cybersecurity adviser said the government is now mapping other similarly exposed sectors, including vaccine cold storage during the flu campaign.
sections.whyItMatters: Food and pharmaceutical supply chains are being probed through the least glamorous door in the building: unpatched building-control systems. No advanced AI required.

sections.heading: Taiwan Puts Private Money Behind the US Chip Supply Chain
sections.body:
Taiwan is raising at least $4 billion through the Taiwan Electrical and Electronic Manufacturers' Association to build an industrial park in Texas, Tom's Hardware reported, citing Bloomberg. The park targets the small and mid-sized Taiwanese suppliers that TSMC and Foxconn depend on but that cannot expand to the US alone. Economics Minister Kung Ming-hsin said the aim is a 'long-term, sustainable supply chain' open to American firms and workers, not just Taiwanese ones. Taipei will also offer loan guarantees and help with US visas, permits and paperwork, and is planning more than one site at $2-4 billion each.

Context: TSMC has already spent $165 billion on its Arizona site and committed a further $100 billion for four more 2nm fabs (Tom's Hardware). The new money is not for fabs - it is for the tooling, materials and packaging firms around them.
sections.whyItMatters: Moving the flagship fab without its supplier base produces an assembly plant that still imports its ecosystem. Taiwan is now funding the harder half of the relocation, and paying for it with private money rather than asking Washington.

sections.heading: China's EUV Light Source: Real Progress, Long Road
sections.body:
Chinese startup Langdao Silex, founded in 2024 by alumni of Tsinghua University's Gas Discharge Plasma Laboratory, demonstrated an extreme ultraviolet light source prototype at the China International Industry Fair in Shanghai with over 15W of output power and 90% domestic components, according to Tom's Hardware citing TrendForce. The company says it needs another three to five years to commercialise. A light source is not a scanner: ASML's production tools operate at far higher power and require an entire optics, stage and metrology industry behind them.

Separately, SK hynix denied playing hardball with Washington over a US NAND fab, telling Tom's Hardware it 'strictly complies with the laws and regulations of all relevant jurisdictions' and that equipment installation at its Dalian facility is 'under authorization from the U.S. government'. Reuters had reported the company was seeking more equipment export approvals for Dalian in exchange for a US fab commitment. The two accounts differ on intent, not on the underlying trade.
sections.whyItMatters: China's lithography effort is advancing in public, step by step, but the gap to a working scanner is still measured in years. Seoul, meanwhile, is bargaining with Washington over equipment licences for its own Chinese plants - a sign that allied firms, not just Beijing, are exposed to US controls.

bottomLine: The day's real news was balance sheets, not breakthroughs. Anthropic put 5% of its equity into a fund it controls, a voluntary answer to the trust problem that avoids legislation; CXMT delivered profits and fell 6-8%; Kioxia is being unwound by margin calls; and the FT reports Microsoft walking away from a data centre deal while SemiAnalysis says local bans barely dent a 38 GW build for 2027. The AI buildout is intact physically and strained financially. Meanwhile the war moved onto the data centre: Ukrainian drones degraded Yandex's consumer services in Russian cities, French hackers turned up supermarket fridges with nothing more sophisticated than an exposed controller, and Taiwan began raising $4bn to move its supplier base - not just its fabs - to Texas.
sources: TechCrunch, BBC News, CNBC, SCMP, Japan Times, Financial Times, The Guardian, POLITICO Europe, Tom's Hardware, SemiAnalysis, Cloudflare, Claroty, TrendForce, Bloomberg (via Tom's Hardware), Reuters (via Tom's Hardware)
